lines: Picture two systems, both of them claiming to handle a network partition correctly.
One of them keeps answering requests on both sides, the whole time the network is split.
The other one goes completely silent on one side, and answers nothing until it's fixed. And somehow, both of them are right.
Here's where I want you to commit to an answer.
A system tells you it's both consistent and available. Fully CA, no asterisks.
The moment a real network partition actually hits that system. What happens?
answer: It's tempting to think a well-engineered system could just stay both, through sheer good design.
But this trade isn't a matter of engineering skill. The instant a real partition happens, the system has to pick one.
Either it keeps answering and risks being wrong, or it refuses and stays correct. There's no third option once the network actually splits.

lines: That word, permanent, is exactly the wrong way to think about this theorem.
The real trade only exists while an actual partition is happening.
Outside of one, there's nothing forcing you to give anything up at all.
So what does the trade actually look like, during a real partition?
One side can answer the request, and risk that the answer is now wrong.
Or it can refuse to answer at all, and guarantee it stays correct. That choice, repeated, is the entire theorem.
Here's the piece the original theorem leaves out entirely.
Even with absolutely no partition happening, there's still a trade going on, every single request.
Wait a little longer and stay perfectly consistent, or answer faster and risk being slightly behind.
One more thing to commit to.
A particular system gives up consistency during a partition, specifically to stay available.
Does that exact same system behave that way even when there's no partition at all?
answer: It's tempting to assume the partition-time choice and the everyday choice are totally separate decisions.
But they usually come from the identical underlying design. A system built to favor availability over consistency during a crisis is, more often than not, built that way on purpose, all the time.
So yes. The same system keeps making the same trade, consistency for speed, whether or not anything is actually broken.

lines: Watch this play out on two real systems, not a hypothetical.
One system, by its own documented design, gives up consistency both during a partition and under completely normal conditions.
A second system, documented just as clearly, refuses to give up consistency either way, and simply pays for it.
Now get specific about what the word partition even means, physically.
A single running process, inside a physical host, inside a rack, inside an availability zone, inside an entire region.
Every one of those is a genuinely real way for something to actually split off from everything else.
Pull the whole topic together.
A real partition forces a choice between staying available and staying consistent. PACELC adds the trade that's sitting there even when nothing is broken.
And both of those choices ultimately come down to real, physical failures you can point to and name.
One last one. A single physical host crashes, somewhere inside one availability zone.
Given everything you just watched about how these domains actually nest inside each other.
Which failure domains does that crash genuinely partition, and which ones does it leave completely untouched?
answer: It's tempting to assume a host failure counts as losing the whole zone it sits in.
But a failure only ever takes down what it's actually contained inside of. That one host, and the process running on it.
The rack holding it, the zone around that rack, and the region the zone sits in: all three of those kept running the entire time, completely unaffected.
